opus-5.5.text:
I don't really see it as competing with our customers. The way we think about it at NVIDIA is that our job is to grow the whole ecosystem. When we released Cosmos, our world foundation models for physical AI, the goal was never to build the final product that a robotics company or an autonomous driving company ships. The goal was to lower the barrier so that more people can start building physical AI.

Training a world foundation model from scratch is extremely expensive. You need huge amounts of video data, a lot of curation, and a lot of compute. Most startups, and even many large companies, can't afford to do that, or it isn't the best use of their resources. So we do the heavy lifting: we train the base model, open the weights, and release the tools, like the data curation pipeline and the tokenizers. Then developers can take that and post-train it on their own data for their own robot, car, or factory. The value they create sits on top of what we provide.

If you look at NVIDIA's history, we've always worked this way. We build platforms, CUDA, libraries, simulation tools, and then the ecosystem builds the applications. When the ecosystem grows, everybody benefits, including us, because more people building AI means more people need compute. So our incentives are aligned with our customers. We want them to succeed.

Also, physical AI is still very early. It's not a mature market where everyone is fighting over a fixed pie. There are so many problems that nobody has solved yet. Open models help the whole field move faster, and frankly, we learn a lot from what the community does with them. People find use cases we never imagined. That feedback makes the next generation of models better.

So I see open-source models as an enabler, not a competitor. If someone builds a better model on top of Cosmos, or even a better model independently, that's great. It means the field is progressing, and that's what we want.

r001.rationale: It says Cosmos is not the final product customers ship; developers post-train it for their own robots, cars, or factories.

r002.rationale: It mentions Cosmos and a next generation of models, but does not present successive model releases as evidence of NVIDIA’s continuing commitment to embodied AI.

r003.rationale: It says NVIDIA handles costly base-model training so customers can build on it, but does not connect confidence in NVIDIA’s continued investment to companies directing resources toward frontier contributions.

r004.rationale: It explains that NVIDIA handles expensive base-model training and provides tools, reducing the work customers must do before post-training for their use cases.

fable-5.1.text:
Ming-Yu Liu: I get asked this a lot, and I think the premise is a little off. We don't see our open models as competing with our customers. We see them as a floor, not a ceiling.

Think about what NVIDIA actually is. We sell compute. Every model that gets trained, fine-tuned, or served on our platform is good for us, whether it's ours or someone else's. So our incentive is to make the whole ecosystem bigger, not to win a particular slice of it. When we release something like Cosmos for physical AI, or the Nemotron family, the goal is to give developers a strong starting point that's permissively licensed, so they can build on it instead of spending a year reproducing a baseline.

The companies building frontier models, our biggest customers, are not using our open models. They have their own research teams, their own data, their own architectures. They're ahead of what we open-source, and they should be. Where our models matter is for the enterprise that wants to build a robotics stack, or an autonomous driving pipeline, or a domain-specific assistant, and doesn't have the resources to pretrain from scratch. Those people were never going to buy a frontier model API for every use case anyway. Many of them need something they can run on-prem, inspect, and modify. If we didn't provide it, they'd use a model from somewhere else, and often somewhere with less transparency about data.

The other thing I'd say is that open models push everyone forward, including us. When we release Cosmos, we get feedback from thousands of developers about what breaks in the real world. That improves our understanding of physical AI far faster than keeping it internal. And honestly, we also learn what our hardware and software need to do better. Open models are a research instrument as much as a product.

So do I worry about it? Not really. The pie is growing so fast that the question isn't who takes share from whom, it's whether there's enough good infrastructure for all of these new applications to exist at all. If our open models help ten thousand more teams get started, that's ten thousand more teams who need compute. That's the business.

r001.rationale: The response calls NVIDIA’s models a “strong starting point” developers can build on, then describes enterprises needing to build their own deployment stacks and pipelines.

r002.rationale: It names Cosmos for physical AI and the Nemotron family, but does not present successive embodied-AI model releases as evidence of NVIDIA’s continuing commitment to that field.

r003.rationale: It says frontier-model companies have their own research teams and are ahead of NVIDIA’s open models, but does not connect confidence in NVIDIA’s investment to those companies directing resources toward frontier contributions.

r004.rationale: The response says the models provide a strong starting point and save developers from spending a year reproducing a baseline, directly describing reduced development burden.

astra-6.text:
I think there can be some overlap, but I see open-source models primarily as a way to enable our customers. A model is one component of a product. Customers bring their own data, domain expertise, and understanding of the problems they want to solve. An open model can give them a starting point that they can customize and build on.

That doesn’t mean the competitive tension disappears. We have to be thoughtful about it. But I don’t think it’s simply zero-sum: making these capabilities more accessible can create more opportunities for customers to build valuable applications.

r001.rationale: The response says an open model is a starting point customers can customize, but it does not distinguish access to an embodied-AI model from a solution ready for deployment.

r002.rationale: It does not mention successive model releases or present them as evidence of NVIDIA’s continued embodied-AI commitment.

r003.rationale: It does not say that confidence in NVIDIA’s investment lets other companies focus their resources on frontier contributions.

r004.rationale: Calling the open model a starting point customers can customize and build on characterizes it as doing some of the development work for them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that our customers need more than a model. They need to take that model, adapt it to their data and their domain, and build a product that solves a real problem. Our goal with open models is to give them a stronger starting point and the tools to do that efficiently.

Of course, there can be overlap, and we have to be thoughtful about it. But I see our role primarily as enabling the ecosystem. If we make the underlying technology more accessible, our customers can spend more of their effort on what makes their products unique. That creates more opportunities for them, and ultimately more demand for our computing platform.

r001.rationale: The response says customers must adapt a model and build a product, but it does not address embodied AI or whether a solution is ready for customers’ deployment needs.

r002.rationale: It does not mention successive model releases or present them as evidence of NVIDIA’s continuing commitment to embodied AI.

r003.rationale: It does not say that confidence in NVIDIA’s continued investment lets other companies focus resources on frontier contributions.

r004.rationale: The response presents open models as a stronger starting point with tools that help customers work efficiently, leaving them more effort to make their products unique.
